join_order.notes: Single k_id resolved at runtime; use CSR to fetch mk rows for this keyword. Deduplicate movie_ids into a bitset over title cardinality (2,528,312).

join_order.probe: movie_companies (per candidate movie via offsets_only on movie_id)
join_order.notes: Build a bitset/byte-array indexed by company_id (size 234,997) marking cn rows with country_code==us_code. Per candidate movie, scan its mc rows; accept movie if ANY mc.company_id is US.

join_order.build: candidate movie set (mk ∩ has US mc)
join_order.notes: For each qualifying movie, iterate ci rows; emit person_id values.
Many pids will have no aka_name rows; offsets_only gives O(1) empty-check. an.person_id = n.id and n.id = ci.person_id collapse to direct index by pid (name has identity id, no filter).

data_structures.candidate_movie_bitset: bitset(2528312) for unique mk-movie_ids that have at least one US mc
data_structures.min_aggregates: two std::string_view holders (min_an_name, min_t_title) updated lexicographically; copy to std::string only when strictly smaller

parallelism.notes: Partition the unique candidate movie list (after mk dedup and US-mc semi-join) across 12 threads. Each thread maintains local (min_an_name, min_t_title); reduce at end. The mk CSR enumeration and US semi-join are cheap and can be done single-threaded to build the candidate set, then parallelize the ci/aka_name probing which is the dominant cost (36M ci rows have hot movies).
